draft.title: Reading tables and graphs
card: A table lists values in rows and columns. Find the row and the column you need, then read where they meet.
On a bar graph or line graph, read the label on each axis first. Then follow the top of a bar, or a point on the line, across to the scale to find its value.
A line graph shows a trend. A line going up means the values rise over time. A line going down means they fall. A flat line means no change.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole. A bigger slice is a bigger share. Example: a pie chart of 200 students shows 25% walk to school. 25% of 200 = 50 students.
draft.remember: Read the labels and scale first, then find the value, trend or share.

a.q: A pie chart shows how 80 students get to school. The bus slice is 50%. How many students take the bus?
a.why: 50% is one half, and half of 80 is 40. Choosing 50 reads the percentage as a number of students, but the chart shows a share of the 80.

b.q: A line graph shows the weekly sales of Mia's café in Dubbo. Sales are $400 in week 1, $500 in week 2, $650 in week 3 and $600 in week 4. Between which two weeks did sales fall?
b.why: Sales went from $650 in week 3 to $600 in week 4, so the line goes down there. The other steps go up. Week 1 to week 4 is a rise overall, from $400 to $600.
b.clue: Look for where the line goes down.

wants.brief: A bar graph of a class's favourite sport: Soccer 12, Netball 8, Cricket 10, Basketball 6, x label Sport, y label Students from 0 to 14 in steps of 2.
wants.why: The student practises reading the axis labels and following the top of each bar across to the scale.

wants.brief: A line graph of visitors on days 1 to 7 (10, 20, 30, 30, 30, 20, 10), x label Day, y label Visitors, with the parts labelled rise, no change and fall.
wants.why: It shows what a line going up, a flat line and a line going down look like.
